metadata.title: From Annotated Data to Training a Computer Vision Model
metadata.purpose: Explain how labeled annotation data is used to train, evaluate, and generalize a YOLO-style loon detection model.
metadata.audience: biologists and conservation researchers new to machine learning

beats.narration_text: Hi, this is Swara Joshi. In this series we've covered the dataset, the metadata, and the annotation stages of the loon computer-vision pipeline. This episode moves into the next major stage: using that labeled data to actually train a computer-vision model, starting with loon detection and counting.

beats.narration_text: The basic idea is simple: we give the model images where loons are already identified and labeled. It looks for patterns in those examples, shape, appearance, visual features, and learns what a loon looks like. Once it's learned from enough examples, we can hand it a new image and ask whether a loon is present.

show.event: Three layers stack how training turns examples into recognition.

layers.title: Labeled examples
layers.sub: Images where loons are already identified and boxed

layers.title: The model finds patterns
layers.sub: Shape, appearance, and visual features that repeat across examples

layers.title: Recognizes new images
layers.sub: Applies what it learned to footage it has never seen

props.caption: The model only knows what the labeled examples taught it.

beats.narration_text: This is where an object-detection model like YOLO comes in, You Only Look Once, built to detect objects efficiently. Instead of just saying a loon is present, it draws a bounding box around it and attaches a confidence score. A future result might read: loon, ninety-two percent confidence, at a specific location in the frame.

show.event: A chip grid lists what an object detector actually returns.

props.sparkLine: What an object detector like YOLO returns
items: You Only Look Once — fast, single-pass detection
A bounding box around the object
A confidence score for the prediction
props.caption: Not just "a loon is present" — where it is, and how sure the model is.

beats.narration_text: There's an important step between our annotations and a trained model: preparing the annotated data into a format the model can actually use. The workflow becomes images, to annotations, to dataset preparation, to model training, to model evaluation, to detection.

show.event: A source flow traces annotations into a trained, evaluated detector.

props.sparkLine: Between annotations and a trained model
props.arcCaption: Annotated data has to be prepared into a format the model can actually train on.
props.settleLine: Every stage before this one exists to feed this pipeline.

beats.narration_text: If our annotations are inconsistent, incomplete, or inaccurate, the model learns from those mistakes. That's why the dataset and annotation stages were never separate from machine learning, they're the foundation the model depends on. Quality upstream is quality downstream.

show.event: A binary branch weighs inconsistent annotations against consistent ones.

data.question: What happens when the model trains on inconsistent or inaccurate annotations?

branches.label: Inconsistent, inaccurate labels
branches.detail: Boxes that vary in tightness, missed or wrong objects
branches.fix: The model learns those mistakes as if they were correct

branches.label: Consistent, accurate labels
branches.detail: Same standard applied across the whole dataset
branches.fix: The model has a reliable foundation to learn from

resolver.label: Consistent, accurate labels
resolver.detail: Dataset and annotation work aren't separate from machine learning, they're the foundation the model depends on

beats.narration_text: We don't just train a model and assume it works. We test it on images it hasn't seen during training, and measure how it performs: missed detections, incorrect detections, and how accurately it locates each loon. Because this is a conservation project, that accuracy genuinely matters.

show.event: A chip grid lists what evaluation actually checks.

props.sparkLine: How we'll know if it actually works
items: Test on images the model hasn't seen
Accuracy of each bounding box location
props.caption: We don't train a model and assume it works, we measure it.

beats.narration_text: A model that performs well on one set of images may not hold up when conditions change. Drone footage varies with altitude, lighting, water reflections, camera angle, weather, and distance to the birds. That's why the dataset needs diverse examples as it grows, not just more of the same.

show.event: Three layers stack the conditions a real model has to handle.

beats.narration_text: The complete vision strings every stage together: raw footage, metadata, annotation, a training dataset, a computer-vision model, then loon detection and counting, feeding a researcher-facing application. The researcher doesn't need to know YOLO is running underneath, they upload footage, run an analysis, and review the results.

show.event: A source flow traces raw footage to the researcher-facing application.

props.arcCaption: The researcher doesn't need to know YOLO is running in the background.
props.settleLine: Upload footage, run an analysis, review the results, that's the whole experience.

beats.narration_text: So the honest state: we don't have a production-ready loon detection model, and we're not claiming one. The goal right now is establishing the complete pipeline, so that once enough suitable loon imagery exists, we can actually train, evaluate, and improve a real model.

show.event: A verdict artifact summarizes the honest state of the pipeline.

artifactLines: We're moving from labeled data into actually training a computer-vision model.
YOLO-style detection returns a location and a confidence score, not just a yes-or-no.
Annotation quality directly determines what the model learns, they aren't separate stages.
There is no production-ready loon detector yet; the goal right now is the complete pipeline, not a finished model.

beats.narration_text: In the next part of the series, we'll go deeper into how YOLO training actually works: training data, validation, model predictions, confidence scores, and how we evaluate whether the model is genuinely learning. If you want to think ahead, here's one question: what result would convince you this model is actually ready for the field?
